opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think one of the biggest issues is that subword tokenizers like BPE are trained on corpora that are overwhelmingly dominated by English and a handful of other high-resource languages. So the vocabulary ends up being really well-suited to those languages, where common words or word pieces get their own compact tokens, but for lower-resource languages, and especially languages that use non-Latin scripts, the same content gets fragmented into many more tokens. Sometimes you're even falling back to individual bytes.

And that has real consequences. If the same sentence takes three or four times as many tokens in, say, Telugu or Burmese as it does in English, then speakers of those languages are effectively paying more if they're using an API that charges per token. They also get less usable context, because the context window fills up faster, and inference is slower. There's been work quantifying these disparities across languages, and they're pretty stark.

Beyond cost and efficiency, there's a modeling issue too. When a word is chopped into pieces that don't line up with meaningful units, like morphemes, the model has a harder time learning good representations for it. So you get a kind of compounding disadvantage: the languages that already have less training data are also represented less efficiently and less meaningfully.

That's a big part of what motivates my interest in moving beyond fixed tokenizers, toward byte-level or tokenizer-free models that can learn how to segment or compress the input themselves. The challenge is that operating directly on bytes makes sequences much longer and more expensive, so a lot of the work is about figuring out how to make those models efficient, for instance by learning to merge or drop information dynamically, so you get the fairness and robustness benefits without paying a huge computational price.

r001.rationale: It says lower-resource languages, especially non-Latin scripts, are fragmented into more tokens than English, resulting in unequal compression rates.

r002.rationale: It explains that a sentence requiring several times as many tokens in languages such as Telugu or Burmese costs speakers more when API pricing is per token.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the big one is that tokenization is fundamentally unfair across languages, and that unfairness gets baked in before the model ever sees a single training example. The way most tokenizers work, something like byte-pair encoding, is that they're trained on a corpus, and they learn to merge frequently occurring sequences into single tokens. So if your corpus is dominated by English, and most of them are, English gets these really nice, efficient, meaningful tokens. Common words become single tokens, you get sensible subword pieces for less common words, and so on.

But then you take that same tokenizer and apply it to, say, Burmese, or Amharic, or even a higher-resource language with a different script, and the tokenizer just doesn't have the vocabulary for it. So it falls back to chopping text into much smaller pieces, sometimes down to individual bytes. The same sentence that takes maybe fifteen tokens in English might take sixty or a hundred tokens in another language. And that has very concrete downstream consequences. The model's context window is effectively shorter for those languages. Inference is more expensive, so users in those languages are literally paying more for the same amount of content. And the model's learning problem is harder, because it's trying to build up meaning from these fragmented, somewhat arbitrary pieces rather than from units that correspond to morphemes or words.

And I'd actually push on the word "arbitrary" there, because I think that's the deeper flaw. The segmentation that a BPE tokenizer produces is driven by frequency statistics, not by anything linguistically principled. So even in English you get these weird splits that don't align with morphology, but in lower-resource languages it's much worse. You're essentially asking the model to learn the language through a distorted lens, and the distortion is worse exactly for the languages that already have the least data.

So part of what I've been interested in is whether we can get away from this fixed, pretrained tokenization step altogether, and let the model learn its own segmentation in a way that can adapt to whatever language or script it's actually processing. Because right now tokenization is this frozen design decision that we make once, up front, and then every language other than the ones we optimized for just has to live with it.

r001.rationale: The response says English gets efficient tokens while other languages may be split into many more tokens, making the same sentence take 60–100 tokens instead of about 15.

r002.rationale: It connects the higher token counts to greater inference expense and says users of those languages pay more for the same amount of content.

astra-6.text:
One important flaw is that tokenization isn’t equally efficient across languages. A tokenizer might represent a common English word with a single token, but break a word in another language into many smaller pieces. So expressing the same thing can require substantially more tokens in one language than in another.

That has practical consequences: users can face higher costs, slower responses, and effectively less room in the context window simply because of the language they’re using. Tokenization can look like a neutral preprocessing step, but it can introduce inequities before the model even starts processing the text.

r001.rationale: The response says tokenizers can split equivalent content in some languages into more tokens, identifying unequal compression across languages.

r002.rationale: It mentions higher costs for users of those languages, but does not explain that per-token API pricing causes the extra tokens to make equivalent content more expensive.

sol-6.1.text: One important flaw is that tokenization isn’t equally efficient across languages. The same content might take relatively few tokens in English but many more in another language, especially one that’s less represented in the tokenizer’s training data. That means speakers of those languages can face higher costs and effectively smaller context windows: they can fit less information into the same token budget. So a seemingly low-level design choice can create real disparities in how people access and use these models.

r001.rationale: It says equivalent content can require relatively few tokens in English but many more in another language, identifying unequal tokenization efficiency across languages.

r002.rationale: It mentions higher costs for speakers of languages that use more tokens, but does not explain that this follows from per-token API pricing.
